---
title: "00 · The JL illusion"
description: "Why relative-distance accuracy can coexist with lost rankings."
---

## The experiment

Generate an isotropic Gaussian cloud, apply one normalized Haar projection,
then compare two diagnostics on the **same map and sample**:

1. the largest relative error over all sample distances;
2. mean Kendall correlation of each query's candidate ranking.

```python
from rpgeom import budget
print(budget(d=10_000, m=200, q=8))
```

The JL event concerns a large baseline of order `d`. Ranking concerns centered
differences of order `sqrt(d)`. A fixed relative tolerance can cover the first
while overwhelming the second.

## The zero-information control

The separation can be absolute. Generate a second low-dimensional Gaussian
cloud independently of the data and scale it to the same population distance
baseline. At JL-scale dimensions, concentration alone can make all labeled
pairwise inequalities hold even though the replacement distances, rankings,
and neighbors are independent of their originals.

![The repository dashboard compares the all-pairs certificate, distance signal,
rankings, nearest neighbors, and two distortion diagnostics. The manuscript
uses only the certificate and distance-signal panels.](../assets/zero_information_jl_dashboard.png){fig-alt="Six-panel zero-information JL experiment dashboard"}

Reproduce the complete dashboard with:

```bash
python experiments/zero_information_jl/run.py \
  --profile full --output artifacts/zero_information_jl
```

The fixed-coordinate Haar implementation is exact for the joint law of the
original and projected distance matrices under isotropy. The shared-pair panel
estimates correlation across repeated independent triples; it does not center
all pairs within one realized cloud.

The generated data also check two points that do not need extra panels. First,
rescaling the replacement to the realized mean distance matches that baseline
to floating-point accuracy without changing any ranking. Second, the observed
failure frequency for disjoint-pair distance ratios agrees with the exact
two-sided $F_{m,d}$ probability. The latter is the finite-sample diagnostic
behind the manuscript's $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$ necessity
argument for independent Gaussian replacement.

::: {.callout-tip}
The surprise is not that JL fails. JL succeeds at exactly what it promises.
The lesson is that satisfying its sampled inequalities does not by itself
force the output to retain sample-specific geometry. Name the downstream
decision before choosing the certificate.
:::
